Learning Objectives
Identify the most common tumors that metastasize to the spine, including histology, imaging
studies, biologic behavior, and typical response to management.
Assess patient prognosis and its role in selecting optimal management.
Develop a strategy to properly diagnose and stage unknown lesions in the spine.
Apply modern multidisciplinary treatment strategies for the management of metastatic spine
tumors.


Overview
Spinal metastatic disease is challenging because various pathologic processes may
occur, including problems related to mechanical instability, neurologic compromise, and
end-organ damage. The sacral, lumbar, thoracic, and cervical spine each contain unique
anatomic features that affect the pathophysiology of disease and management;
however, tumor histology factors, host factors, and other factors also are critical in
selecting proper management for metastatic spine disease. Few disciplines are evolving
as quickly because our understanding of patient prognosis and multidisciplinary
management evolves in parallel to progress in surgical, radiotherapy, and medical
oncology fields.1
Epidemiology
Metastatic spine disease typically occurs in individuals older than 40 years.
The spine is the most common site of bone metastasis, with the thoracic spine being the most
common spinal site, followed by the lumbar spine and then cervical spine (Figure 1).
Although 60% to 70% of patients with metastatic cancer have detectable spinal disease (90%
using postmortem studies), only 10% to 20% become symptomatic.
Most common primary cancer sites that metastasize to bone are breast, prostate, lung, kidney,
and thyroid.


Epidemiology
The spine is the most common bony site of metastatic tumors to bone, with the thoracic
spine being the most common subregion.2 Although patients are not always
symptomatic, some spinal involvement is ubiquitous in patients with known metastases.
The epidemiology and histologic spectrum of tumors that metastasize to the spine are
similar to those for the extremities. The most common tumor types are myeloma,
lymphoma, breast, lung, prostate, renal, and thyroid. Increased diagnostic prevalence,
more effective cancer treatment options, and an aging population increase relevance to
the field of spinal metastatic disease.
Classification Systems

Classification schema exist to delineate multiple issues in metastatic spine disease.
Extent of tumor (Weinstein-Boriani-Biagini)
Extent of cord compression (metastatic epidural spinal cord compression [MESCC] scale)
Mechanical instability (Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score)
Neurologic grading (multiple frameworks)

Classification Systems
The classification and characterization of spinal metastatic disease involve various
factors: defining the anatomic extent of tumor, describing the extent of spinal cord
compression, predicting mechanical instability, describing neurologic status, and
predicting patient life expectancy. Consideration of each of these factors is useful in the
field of spinal metastatic disease because it aids communication among practitioners,
research, determination of life expectancy/prognosis, and decision making for
treatment.
The Weinstein-Boriani-Biagini classification system is useful for primary and metastatic
tumors because it offers a precise method to describe the anatomic extent of tumor.3
Based on an axial view of the spine, this system uses a radial clockface around the
vertebral bone, with depth modifiers indicating extraosseous, intraosseous, epidural,
and intradural extent of disease. This system helps describe the tumor extent and allows
the surgeon to consider the surgical approach to be used.
Bilsky and Smith4 first published the MESCC scale. The MESCC scale describes the extent
of tumor impingement on the cord by distinguishing entirely intraosseous (grade 0),
epidural (grade 1a: no thecal sac impingement; grade 1b: thecal sac impingement with
no cord impingement; grade 1c: spinal cord abutment without compression), and cord-
deforming (grade 2: cord compressed but spinal fluid visible; grade 3: cord compressed
with no spinal fluid visible) processes. The MESCC also guides management because
high-grade compression (grade 2 and grade 3) most commonly is appropriate for
surgical decompression.

The Spinal Instability Neoplastic Score uses the location of tumor, lytic characteristics,
collapse of bone, deformity of bone, integrity of posterior elements, and presence of
mechanical pain to predict mechanical instability and the need for surgical
management.5 Unfortunately, many tumors fall into the indeterminate category of this
scale, and the scale is most commonly used to validate intuitively surgical or nonsurgical
ends of the presentation spectrum.
Various methods and grading scales are available to assess neurologic function. These
include measures of acute spinal cord injury, such as the American Spinal Injury
Association (ASIA) scale or the Frankel classification, both of which describe motor and
sensory function below an injury level. In addition, patients with or without neurologic
involvement should be classified via more indirect scales of neurologic and physical
function using performance status systems, such as the Eastern Cooperative Oncology
Group or the Karnofsky scales, both of which describe physical and ambulatory daily
function. These are particularly important to prognosis.
Applied Anatomy and Biomechanics
Cervical Spine
Greater mobility
Relative to other spinal regions, more biomechanic stress on the posterior bony elements
(facet/lateral mass complex) and ligamentous tension band
Spinal cord
Unique anatomy: vertebral arteries, occiput-C1-C2 complex

Cervical Spine
The cervical spine contains unique anatomic features that are relevant to metastatic
tumors. First, this zone is relatively mobile compared with the remainder of the spine.
The unique occiput-C1 articulation involving a spherical condyle/dish arrangement
allows for high degrees of flexion if combined with the subaxial spine, as does the
unique C1-C2 articulation through the dens for rotation. If these articulations are
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:44 PM
AAOS | Metastatic Bone Disease to the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001077
5/44

disrupted by tumor, pathologic hypermobility may result. Also, compared with other
spinal zones, the cervical spine posterior elements bear relatively more biomechanic
load than the anterior column, with the facet/lateral mass complex assuming more of
the compression stress and the posterior ligamentous complex assuming more tension
in flexion.6 Therefore, posterior element involvement by tumor is particularly
destabilizing. Lastly, the vertebral arteries and the motor nerve roots of the cervical
spine frequently complicate proper eradication of tumor, and subtotal resection may be
required if these structures are involved.
Thoracic Spine
Relatively immobile except at cervicothoracic and thoracolumbar junctions
Thoracic root sacrifice facilitates 360° decompression and reconstruction.
Vertebral bodies are protected by the rib cage and the sternal complex.
Longest latency of pain to collapse
Most sparse spinal cord blood supply
Unique anatomy: surrounding viscera

Thoracic Spine
The thoracic spine is relatively immobile. The vertebrae are protected by the sternal-rib
complex; therefore, they tolerate more bony destruction than more mobile segments.
The exception is at the superior and inferior junctions of the thoracic spine, at which
transitional zones to more mobile segments are particularly prone to neoplastic
instability. In addition, the thoracic spine has several unique features involving neural,
visceral, and vascular anatomy. For example, compression of the thoracic nerve roots
may cause sensory pain but no clinically detectable motor deficits, and these roots may
be readily sacrificed without appreciable motor loss. However, the thoracic spinal cord
has the least redundant and most tenuous blood supply to the spinal cord, which should
be considered and possibly interrogated via angiography in planning extensive
approaches.7

In addition, the great vessels; lung fields; esophagus; and upper abdominal structures,
such as the kidney, may be compromised by local tumor advancement and must be
protected during surgical management.
Lumbar Spine
Mobile
Spinal cord ends at approximately T12/L1.
Thecal sac below the conus can be manipulated more than at the cord level and is more
tolerant to epidural compression.
Preservation of the lower extremity motor roots is critical in resecting or reconstructing
tumors.
Lumbosacral-pelvic alignment is critical to consider in reconstruction.

Lumbar Spine
Lumbar spine anatomy also is relatively mobile. Bony destruction at the high-stress,
high-motion segments near the lumbosacral junction or the thoracolumbar junction may
cause pathologic instability; however, the lumbar spine is more tolerant to mechanical
instability or epidural tumor advancement because it does not contain the spinal cord
proper. Although the lumbar motor roots must be preserved to retain ambulatory
function, they may be carefully manipulated more than the spinal cord itself during
surgical management, allowing for more extensive all-posterior resections; however, the
cauda equina nerve roots must pass through the lumbar spine on their path toward the
sacrum. The base of the spine at the lumbosacral-pelvic articulation is critical for overall
spinal alignment, and sagittal deformity principles should be considered in planning
lumbar spine reconstruction.8
Sacral Spine
Sacral nerve roots (especially S2 and S3) are critical for bowel, bladder, and sexual function. S1
is the last motor root in the spine.

Complex three-dimensional anatomy includes ventral and dorsal oblique bony
neuroforaminae, sigmoid sacroiliac articulations, sacral-spinous and sacral-tuberous
ligaments, and iliolumbar ligaments.
Tumors in this zone may disrupt or cause fracture of the spinopelvic connection and require
spanning spinopelvic fixation.

Sacral Spine
Sacral zones of the spine are fixed and immobile but comprise a critical connection
between the mobile spine and the pelvis. Therefore, sacral destruction, especially
around the critical alar structures of S1, may result in spinopelvic discontinuity. In
addition, the sacral nerve roots are responsible for plantar foot motor and sensory
function (S1) and bowel, bladder, and sexual function. The S2 and S3 roots are the main
determinants of these functions, and loss of roots below S3 usually results in preserved
function.9
Neurology
95% or more metastatic disease to the spine occurs in the extradural space; however,
intradural involvement is possible.
Distinguishing root-level from cord-level injury is critical to prognosis and treatment planning.
Neural injury may result from direct compression, mechanical instability, or vascular
compromise.

Neurology
Several mechanisms are possible for neurologic injury in patients with metastatic spine
disease. The most common is epidural direct compression; however, mechanical
instability or vascular compromise also may lead to neural injury. In planning treatment,
knowledge of the trajectory (acute versus chronic, evolving versus stable), nature (root-

9/3/26, 4:44 PM
AAOS | Metastatic Bone Disease to the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001077
8/44

level versus cord-level injury), and density (partial versus complete, severity and
distribution of root dysfunction) is critical.
Vascular Anatomy
Vascular considerations are relevant to spinal metastatic disease.
Vertebral arteries in cervical approaches
Artery of Adamkiewicz in the thoracic spine
Vena cava/aorta/segmental vasculature in circumferential approaches
Hypervascularity of certain histologies (thyroid/renal) may demand preoperative embolization.

Vascular Anatomy
Vascular issues also are relevant. The surgeon must first navigate critical vascular
structures, such as the vertebral arteries, great vessels, and segmental vessels
(especially the key supply to the spinal cord, [ie, artery of Adamkiewicz]7). However, the
surgeon also must recognize that neovascularity is a key determinant of metastatic
growth potential, and that surgical manipulation of metastatic tumors, especially
histologies such as renal cell, thyroid, and hepatocellular or metastatic
lymphangiosarcoma, may result in difficult-to-control bleeding. Therefore, preoperative
angiography and embolization frequently are used to limit surgical bleeding and provide
additional neoadjuvant local control.
Surrounding Viscera
Consider not only metastatic disease impinging on local structures but also local extension of
primary visceral disease from these organs into the spine.
Tracheoesophageal complex
Lungs
Colon/small bowel


Surrounding Viscera
Because the spinal column lies at the most axial or central core of the human body,
pathologic processes may radially affect surrounding organ systems adjacent to the
spine, such as the esophagus, lungs, kidneys, and rectum. Surgeons must recognize that
primary tumors originating in these same structures may progress locally into the spinal
bones or neurologic elements, and multidisciplinary surgical procedures may be
required.
Etiology of Spinal Metastatic Disease
Two main hypotheses
1889: Paget’s seed and soil hypothesis—Tumor cells can survive and grow in addition to the
compatible end-organ environment.
1928: Ewing’s circulation theory—Tumors colonize particular organs because of the routes of
blood flow from the primary site.
Organs are passive receptacles.
Batson plexus—Valveless plexus of veins around the spine allows tumor cells to travel to
the vertebral bodies (eg, prostate metastases).
Mediators of bone destruction in metastatic disease include:
Tumor necrosis factors
Transforming growth factors
1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D3
Parathyroid hormone–related protein secreted by tumors
Pathophysiology/molecular mechanisms
Metastatic cascade
Primary tumor cells proliferate, stimulate angiogenesis, and cross the basement membrane
into capillaries/bloodstream.
Tumor cells disseminate, arrest in distant capillary bed, adhere, and extravasate into end-
organ environment (integrins, cadherins, matrix metalloproteinases).
Tumor cells proliferate and interact with local host cells via growth factors (transforming
growth factor-ß, insulin-like growth factor, fibroblast growth factor, bone morphogenetic
protein).

Receptor activator of nuclear factor-ĸB ligand (RANKL)/osteoprotegerin
Tumor cells do not destroy bone; cytokines from the tumor stimulate osteoclasts or
osteoblasts to destroy or generate new bone, respectively.
RANKL pathway: Osteoblasts/stromal cells secrete RANKL, which causes an increase in
osteoclast precursors and eventually results in increased bone destruction.
Osteoprotegerin is a decoy receptor that binds to RANKL and inhibits an increase in
osteoclasts.
Sclerostin
Fracture healing in pathologic bone
Likelihood of pathologic fracture healing: lymphoma > multiple myeloma > breast carcinoma
> lung carcinoma > renal carcinoma
Other physiologic disruptions
Calcium metabolism—Hypercalcemia is present in 10% to 30% of patients.
Common with lung and breast cancer metastasis
Disruption in calcium metabolism may be caused by renal dysfunction in the context of
increased calcium release in the serum; however, the exact mechanism is unknown.
Early symptoms: polyuria/polydipsia, anorexia, weakness, easy fatigability
Late symptoms: irritability, depression, coma, profound weakness, nausea/vomiting,
pruritus, vision abnormalities
Management requires aggressive hydration and intravenous diphosphonate therapy.
Hematopoiesis—Normocytic/normochromic anemia is common with breast, prostate, lung,
and thyroid cancer metastasis.
Thromboembolic disease
Patients with malignancy have increased thromboembolic risk (Virchow triad: stasis,
endothelial injury, hypercoagulability)
Prophylaxis after complex spinal surgery generally is required; however, the physician must
balance the risk of epidural hematoma or other hemorrhage.

Etiology of Spinal Metastatic Disease
Sclerostin is produced by osteocytes to maintain osteoblasts in a quiescent state until
activated, such as in times of fracture. Some tumors (myeloma and some breast cancers)
produce sclerostin, which allows them to suppress osteoblastic activity.

https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001077
11/44

Bony healing is possible after cancer cells have been removed surgical or via radiation
therapy. Naturally, pathologic fractures caused by tumors that are sensitive to
irradiation (myeloma) are more likely to heal than those that are less sensitive to
irradiation (lung).
The process of a primary tumor proliferating, gaining access to the systemic circulation,
and re-proliferating at a distant site is complex and has been subject to many
mechanistic theories, such as the seed and soil hypothesis (Paget) or the circulation
theory (Ewing).10 The exact nature of this process remains unknown, and even the most
intriguing theories do not fully explain the disease process. For example, prostate
metastases were originally thought to have a predilection for the spine because of the
Batson plexus, a valveless venous network directly communicating prostate drainage
with the epidural venous plexus. However, if this was the only explanation, the pattern
of prostate metastases would follow venous networks exclusively; however, the
observed distribution of metastases is more broad and unpredictable. Most likely,
physical and molecular factors combine to determine the metastatic event.11
After a tumor finds a distant growth site and begins to proliferate, it may cause bony
destruction via a variety of mechanisms; however, most are indirect. Tumor cytokines
hijack the bone’s growth/resorption mechanisms via molecules such as parathyroid-
hormone-related peptide or RANKL analogs. These disruptive processes allow tumor
invasion and destruction of bony tissue, disruption of normal marrow functions, such as
hematopoiesis, and other deleterious effects. These same molecular mechanisms make
pathologic fracture healing difficult without local control or eradication of tumor tissue in
the bone.
Natural History
Mean time from cancer diagnosis to spinal metastasis is 32 months.
Mean time from spinal metastasis diagnosis to spinal fracture is 27 months.
Investigation of mechanical or nonmechanical back pain is critical in patients with metastatic
cancer.


Natural History
The natural history of metastatic spine disease is progressive. Although metastatic
carcinoma of the spine implies a poor prognosis, patients who survive generally
experience a cascade of asymptomatic spinal involvement, followed by nonmechanical
back or neck pain and then progression of symptoms to mechanical pain or neurologic
compromise.12 In patients with known metastatic cancer, unexplained back or neck
complaints should be investigated thoroughly.
Prognosis
Overview
Median 1 year survival rate is ~50% for all patients treated surgically for spinal metastases.
Epidural disease is associated with a shortened expected survival interval.
Determinants of Mean Survival
Histology and prior management
Performance status/neurologic status
Patient age
Extent of spinal or visceral metastases
Nutritional status/laboratory results

Determinants of Mean Survival
Prognosis is one of the most important and difficult aspects of caring for patients with
metastatic spine disease. Determining expected survival accurately is critical to
informing treatment options, optimizing quality of life, and executing end-of-life
planning.13-15 Historically, primary tumor histology alone was thought to be the best
predictor of survival; however, current predictors have improved remarkably to include
many other factors that influence survival, such as the extent of disease, patient age,
performance status, prior management, nutrition, and serum laboratory results.

Unfortunately, the study of prognosis is a moving target because the effectiveness of
cancer treatment options is evolving in parallel and markedly changing expected
survivals. For example, current targeted therapies, such as PD-1/PD-L1 inhibitors, have
elicited drastic responses in some patients with metastatic lung cancer, which is
associated with a poor prognosis in most patients. Consequently, surgeons must apply
predictive models in the context of all available factors for the patient being treated.
Predictive models are not meant to make decisions for clinicians or patients, and their
use demands a complete understanding of their advantages and potential
disadvantages.
Scoring Systems
Tokuhashi scale
Tomita scale
Modified Bauer scale
New England Spinal Metastases Score
Spinal Oncology Research Group algorithm

Scoring Systems
Many distinct prognostic scoring systems have been used in the field of spinal metastatic
disease, each of which is associated with advantages and disadvantages. Three systems
are most commonly used and cited. The Tokuhashi scale considers the extent of spinal
and extraspinal metastases, primary histology, and performance status and is the only
system to consider neurologic status.16 The scale predicts survival in 6-month intervals
up to 1 year, and, therefore, has a ceiling effect for favorable prognoses. The Tomita
scale is simpler to use and more generalizable, considering tumor biology (not named
histology) and spinal and extraspinal disease extent. The original description of the
Tomita scale also included survival estimates for very short (<3 months) and very long
(>2 years) survival.17 The modified Bauer scale considers tumor histology and spinal and
extraspinal sites and is most similar to the Tomita scale.18

More recently, several multicenter groups have attempted to improve upon these scales.
The New England Spinal Metastasis Score uses the modified Bauer scale and adds
performance status and nutritional assessment via albumin level to determine the
likelihood of 1-year survival. The New England Spinal Metastasis Score also has been
validated to predict 30-day mortality, major systemic complications, and failure to rescue
(mortality rate after a sentinel complication).19 Similarly, the Spinal Oncology Research
Group constructed a machine learning–based algorithm that considers histology,
functional status, patient age, tumor stage, and multiple laboratory values.20 Many
validation studies have been performed using these two more modern scales; however,
additional studies are necessary to determine the preferred scale.
Evaluation/Diagnosis
Patient History
Progressive pain that occurs at rest or at night (nonmechanical tumor growth) and with
standing or walking (mechanical)
Constitutional symptoms (weight loss, fatigue, loss of appetite)
Personal or family history of cancer
History of symptoms or risk factors related to possible primary sites (hematuria, shortness of
breath, hot/cold intolerance, goiter, breast mass, smoking history, last mammogram,
occupational exposure)
Primary tumors may metastasize quickly or take 10 to 15 years or more to metastasize (breast,
renal, prostate)

Patient History
History taking for patients with back or neck complaints in whom systemic cancer is
suspected should be driven by the most likely diagnoses and their pathophysiology. For
example, in a patient with a history of prostate cancer, questions surrounding urinary
habits, last serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) test, and prior treatment are
appropriate. For patients without a known history of cancer, questions targeting the
most common histologies (breast, renal, thyroid, prostate, lung, lymphoma, myeloma),

such as the presence of a breast or neck mass; hematuria; smoking history; and
occupational exposure are advisable. General symptoms of cancer, such as fatigue,
weight loss, and other constitutional symptoms, should be elucidated. Lastly, a complete
understanding of the difference between mechanical and nonmechanical pain
symptoms and lower and upper motor neuron complaints should be obtained.
Many patients who present for evaluation have known metastatic disease and have been
treated via multiple chemotherapeutic agents. This is an important aspect of the patient
history because some chemotherapeutics can cause peripheral neuropathy. Peripheral
neuropathy may mask neurologic signs or symptoms related to spinal metastasis.
General Physical Examination
Gait disturbance (limp, inability to stand, shuffling, or broad-based myelopathy gait)
Pain with spinal range of motion
Assess for breast, prostate, thyroid, or abdominal mass or regional adenopathy.

General Physical Examination
The general physical examination of patients in whom spinal metastasis is suspected
should focus on gait, ambulatory status, range of motion, and masses that may indicate
a primary tumor. A systems-based complete examination is advisable. Perhaps the most
important aspect of the physical examination is the neurologic component.
Neurologic Examination
Strength and Sensation
0 to 5 motor grading scale for all myotomes
Sensory examination for light touch, sharp, and dull for all dermatomes
Upper Motor Neuron Findings and Reflexes

Deep tendon reflexes
Babinsky, clonus, inverted, and Hoffman reflexes
Sacral reflexes: rectal tone, bulbocavernosus
Classification
ASIA/Frankel grade
Performance status

Neurologic Examination
Patients with metastatic spine disease should be assessed their comprehensive detailed
motor (0 to 5 myotome scale), sensory (sharp/dull/light touch absent or diminished), and
reflex function (deep tendon, upper motor neuron, and sacral root reflexes) because
patients may present with a wide array of complete or incomplete, acute or chronic, and
upper or lower motor neuron processes. In addition, patients with metastatic spine
disease often present with multifocal disease, which may make the examination complex
or confusing.
Imaging Studies
Goals
Evaluate the tumor effect on spinal soft tissues, bony elements, and neurologic structures
Diagnosis: determine the primary cell of origin
Staging: stage after a diagnosis is obtained
Surveillance: monitor disease after management
For prognostic systems

Goals
Imaging studies in patients with metastatic spine disease serves various purposes and
encompasses various modalities. Characterization of the bony and soft-tissue extent of
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:44 PM
AAOS | Metastatic Bone Disease to the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001077
17/44

the tumor in the spine is one goal of spinal imaging; however, assessment of spinal
mechanical alignment, diagnostic evaluation of body organ systems to evaluate for
primary tumor, staging of already-diagnosed disease, and surveillance of managed
disease also are important goals of imaging studies.
Plain Radiography
Format
Full-length standing AP and lateral radiographs
Sitting radiographs if the patient is not able to stand
Appearance
Osteolytic (most bone metastases): lung, thyroid, kidney, gastrointestinal
Osteoblastic: prostate, bladder
Mixed osteolytic/osteoblastic: breast
Winking owl sign is loss of unilateral pedicle contour on AP radiographs (Figure 2).
Metastatic carcinoma to the spine spares the intervertebral disk.

bone, manifested by loss of the pedicle (arrow) and described as the winking owl sign. Such a
finding on conventional radiographs warrants additional imaging studies to better visualize the


Plain Radiography
Plain radiography is an important initial imaging modality because it screens for obvious
bony destruction. Plain radiographs are the best imaging study to assess mechanical
SEND FEEDBACK
9/3/26, 4:44 PM
AAOS | Metastatic Bone Disease to the Spine
https://rock.aaos.org/coursecontent.aspx?id=6001077
19/44

alignment because most advanced imaging studies are obtained with the patient in the
supine position. Full-length standing AP and lateral radiographs are obtained for
completeness. Qualitatively, the practitioner should evaluate for lytic (most tumors),
blastic (prostate, uroendothelial), or mixed (breast) patterns. A disadvantage of plain
radiography of the spine is that abdominal and thoracic viscera often obscure fine or
subtle details. For example, the winking owl sign describes the obliteration of a unilateral
pedicle shadow on AP radiographs; however, this is a late finding that necessitates
advanced bone loss to be observed on radiographs. Therefore, normal appearing
radiographs should not stop the investigator from obtaining advanced imaging studies,
especially if pain at rest or neurologic complaints are reported.
Advanced Imaging Studies
Computed Tomography
CT offers the best delineation of bone contour and cortical defects.
CT myelography is a second-choice imaging study in patients with contraindications to MRI.
CT of the chest, abdomen, and pelvis is critical in the diagnostic work up of an unknown adult
lesion because it commonly elucidates the primary organ tumor.
Magnetic Resonance Imaging
MRI of the entire spine is the standard of care in patients with metastatic spine disease (Figure
3).
MRI elucidates the status of soft tissues, tumor extension, and neurologic elements.
Full diagnostic study of the area of interest with limited full-length sagittal T2-weighted images
usually is sufficient.
MRI findings in patients with a pathologic (as opposed to insufficiency) fracture include:
High signal intensity extending into the pedicle on T2-weighted images
Soft-tissue mass

Advanced Imaging Studies
The advanced imaging modality of choice is determined by the goals of the physician.
For example, CT of the spine is the best imaging modality for assessing bony detail but is
not the best imaging modality to evaluate the neural elements or soft-tissue extent of
tumor. CT is particularly useful for evaluating the chest, abdomen, and pelvis in the
diagnostic evaluation for a primary tumor and in patients in whom MRI is
contraindicated if used in combination with myelography.
Contrast-enhanced MRI is the preferred imaging modality for evaluating spinal tumors.
In addition to diagnostic study at the region of interest, full-length (occiput to sacrum)
sagittal T2-weighted images should be obtained for most patients diagnosed with a
spinal tumor because synchronous metastases are relatively common. Most tumors
appear as bright lesions on T2-weighted images and also enhance on T1-weighted
gadolinium enhanced images given their hypervascularity. MRI is especially useful in
delineating normal tissue planes that contain fat (best observed on non–fat-suppressed
T1-weighted images). The spinal cord, cerebrospinal fluid, nerve roots, blood vessels,
and other soft-tissue structures are best studied in relation to neoplastic tissue via MRI.
A frequent clinical dilemma involves distinguishing pathologic fracture from osteoporotic
or insufficiency fracture. MRI is especially useful in this regard because pathologic
fractures typically contain enhancing soft-tissue masses, cortical permeation, and high
signal intensity in the pedicles (T2-weighted images), whereas insufficiency fractures do
not reveal such these findings.

Pathologic Diagnosis
Tissue diagnosis remains the preferred method for diagnosis in spinal metastases;
however, most diagnoses can be made via a patient history, physical examination,

Radiation Therapy
Conventional external beam irradiation has played an important role in the
management of metastatic spine disease. The landmark study by Patchell et al23
demonstrated that surgical treatment in combination with conventional external beam
irradiation was better than radiation therapy alone in preserving or regaining
ambulatory status for patients with MESCC. However, the disadvantage of conventional
external beam irradiation is dosing to nontarget organs and normal tissues. The off-
target effect of radiation therapy limits the dosage that can be delivered safely. For
example, the spinal cord has a lifetime tolerance of 55 Gy of irradiation. Similarly, other
adjacent structures, such as the bowel and esophagus, have limited tolerance to
irradiation. Therefore, the dosage of nonconformal, conventional irradiation is limited by
the toxicity imparted on normal/noncancerous tissue. Some cancers, such as lung
carcinoma, rectal carcinoma, and metastatic sarcoma, cannot be effectively eradicated
via these limited dosages. Therefore, more precise forms of irradiation using shaping
technology have emerged. These photon-based modalities, such as stereotactic
radiosurgery or intensity-modulated radiation therapy, can precisely deliver irradiation
to the target with minimal off-target dosing. The advantage of this technology is higher
dosing to the pathologic tissue with less off-target effect. The irradiation dosage can be

Indications
Many patients with tumors in the spine do not require surgical treatment because they
present with a stable mechanical structure and without progressive neurologic decline.
The most reliable method to consider in deciding to surgically manage a spine tumor is
the neurologic, oncologic, mechanical, systemic decision framework, which was first
described formally by Laufer et al.24 This framework reminds the physician to consider
four distinct factors: neurologic, oncologic, mechanical, and systemic. Although the care
of each patient should be individualized, tumors that are mechanically stable, without
neurologic decline, involving histologies sensitive to systemic therapy or radiation
therapy, in patients with comorbidities that prohibit surgical treatment, generally should
be management nonsurgically. However, patients with neurologic injury, mechanical
instability, and non-sensitive histology who are physically robust may be better
candidates for surgical treatment. Determining the extent of surgical treatment in each
patient is one of the great challenges in the management of metastatic spine tumors.
Emerging literature shows that patients who undergo surgical treatment may be able to
maintain function and independence longer than those who undergo nonsurgical
treatment. However, these benefits do not always occur in individuals who undergo
surgical treatment after failed nonsurgical treatment, and the adverse effects of
chemotherapy and radiation therapy may increase the risk of postoperative morbidity.

Dorsal laminectomy can be performed from the cervical spine to the sacrum in any
patient in whom spinal canal decompression is required or in whom the predominance
of tumor burden is dorsal. This technique is intuitive and straightforward for most spinal
surgeons; however, this technique should not be used in isolation if ventral or
circumferential tumor resection or decompression is required, because dorsal-only
decompression will not allow neural element driftback in most patients.
Anterior cervical corpectomy also is an intuitive approach for most spinal surgeons. The
standard Smith-Robinson technique is used for access, and a standard diskectomy is
performed above and below the area of interest. This is especially useful because it
helps the surgeon visualize normal uncovertebral anatomy for proper orientation of the
resection trough. Curettes or high-speed drills are used to remove tumor and bone in a
channel that is approximately as wide as the uncus-to-uncus distance (typically 17 to 18
mm), taking care to not lose orientation and extend the trough laterally in the area in
which the vertebral arteries lie. Reconstruction via bone or synthetic cages then is
performed.
Costotransversectomy is one of the most important approaches for the management of
metastatic spine disease. In this approach, an all-posterior midline exposure is
performed with unilateral or bilateral exposure of the medial 4 to 5 cm of the ribs,
depending on the tumor extent. Dorsal laminectomy is performed, with ligation of
sacrificial thoracic or nonmotor nerve roots. The medial 4 to 5 cm of the ribs at all
involved segments and usually the first caudal uninvolved segment are resected.
Segmental vasculature is ligated or otherwise controlled, and blunt dissection is
performed down the lateral vertebral body wall. This allows for placement of malleable
retractors and complete resection of all posterior elements; diskectomy; and anterior
body resection via a single incision, all-posterior approach. Anterior column
reconstruction also is performed via this anterolateral working window.
Formal open retroperitoneal/transthoracic corpectomy affords excellent access and
anterior decompression but requires a more extended, staged procedure in most
patients and may be associated with increased morbid. Regardless, the technique is

Reconstruction after surgical management of metastatic spine disease encompasses
various anatomic regions, material types, and goals. The first consideration is whether
tumor removal or nerve decompression has left the spine in a mechanically unstable
state, requiring stabilization. Disruption of the posterior ligamentous complex at the
junctional spinal zone, removal of more than 50% of the bilateral facets, and anterior
column deletion are common reasons to consider reconstruction. Next, surgeons must
determine whether to fuse the spine. Given the frailty of the host, frequent use of
irradiation, and systemic treatments, successful arthrodesis rates are low, and achieving
solid arthrodesis does not appear to affect survival, the need for revision surgery, or
ambulatory status.27 Surgeons also should take care with the implant materials, which
may include various metallic, bone, or cement materials or other synthetic materials,
such as polyether ether ketone or carbon-fiber. Radiolucent implants facilitate imaging
surveillance and may have less effect on irradiation planning and delivery.
